openers.late-ordovician-epoch: The Late Ordovician begins with continents on the move and ends in catastrophe. Terranes split from Gondwana, Avalonia struck Baltica, and huge eruptions blanketed Laurentia in ash. Impacts scarred Sweden and Estonia, and a brief warming built reef mounds across Europe. Arthropods left the oldest clear evidence of animals on land. Then extinction rates began to climb, several million years before a great glaciation.
openers.silurian-period: The Silurian is the period of fish and the first green coasts. Jawed fish diversified into placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish, while armored jawless fish reached their height. Nematophytes, strange land organisms, towered over the small plants beside them. Old groups bowed out, from asaphid trilobites to eocrinoid echinoderms. Far to the south, the Rheic Ocean opened to its greatest width, about 4,000 km.
openers.llandovery-epoch: The Llandovery opens on a recovering world. Its base lies at Dob's Linn in southern Scotland, just after the end-Ordovician extinctions, and as melting ice re-flooded the shelves, life rebounded. Reefs spread, land plants covered much of the land surface, and the oldest unambiguous jawed vertebrates appear in China. Milder glaciations came and went. Meanwhile Baltica and Laurentia began their slow collision in the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny.
openers.wenlock-epoch: The Wenlock is short and turbulent. It opens with the Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, which lasted about 200,000 years. Carbon and oxygen isotopes swung after it, and two more crises followed, the Lundgreni and Mulde events. Yet the epoch also saw the first scorpions and the start of a long rise in oxygen, as vascular plants and fungi began to colonize dry land.

reviews.late-ordovician-epoch: The Late Ordovician shows a full world undone by ice. Continents collided, terranes drifted, and arthropods began moving onto land as extinction rates crept up through the Katian. Then a sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary spread ice over Gondwana, and sea level fell sharply. The first pulse of extinction came with the cold, and the second with spreading anoxia as the ice retreated. It was the first of the Big Five mass extinctions, yet diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.
reviews.silurian-period: The Silurian is a turnover story. Ancient groups that had survived since the Cambrian or Ordovician, among them asaphid trilobites, nektaspids, eocrinoids and paracrinoids, made their last appearance. In their place, jawed fish diversified while jawless fish declined. Stromatoporoid sponges branched into most of their orders, and nematophytes stood tall on land. Through it all, Armorica drifted north and the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width.
reviews.llandovery-epoch: The Llandovery is the recovery after the end-Ordovician extinctions. As sea level rose again, surviving groups rebounded, and Lazarus taxa returned from refuges. Reefs spread, land plants covered much of the land, and the first vascular plants, Cooksonia, appeared by the epoch's end. Jawed fish emerged in China, from acanthodian-grade forms to the first bony fish. Meanwhile the Taconic orogeny ended and the Scandian collision of Baltica and Laurentia began.
reviews.wenlock-epoch: The Wenlock tied extinctions to swings in climate and carbon. The Ireviken event, the Lundgreni crisis and the Mulde event each struck, linked to cooling, anoxia or falling sea level. Each left a carbon isotope excursion in the rocks. At the same time, land life was transforming the planet: vascular plants and fungi spread, oxygen began rising toward modern levels, and falling CO2 cooled the climate.

camb-085.title: The Ollo de Sapo magmatic event
camb-085.text: A mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep in the Earth, fed magma into northwestern Gondwana. It struck from the Furongian to the end of the Early Ordovician, about 495–470 Ma. That region is now the Iberian Peninsula. The Ollo de Sapo event ran long enough to span the boundary between two periods.

ordo-043.title: The Hunic terranes split from Gondwana
ordo-043.text: Behind a line of volcanoes, the crust stretched and tore. This back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes, a group of crustal blocks, away from Gondwana in the late Ordovician. The split opened the Paleo-Tethys Ocean behind them. The terranes then began moving north toward Euramerica, a journey that would carry them to the future Europe.

ordo-044.title: The Kazakh terranes gather into Kazakhstania
ordo-044.text: Near the equator lay an archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, the Kazakh terranes. They merged as part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt. Crust was added to paleo-Kazakhstan until the accretion was complete, by the end of the Ordovician and Silurian. Another account places their final assembly into Kazakhstania in the late Silurian.

ordo-045.title: The last agnostid trilobites
ordo-045.text: Agnostids, a group of small trilobites, had already declined sharply across the Cambrian–Ordovician transition. The last of them died out in the Late Ordovician. The Ordovician mass extinction ended them, along with the once-successful Telephinidae, closing two long-lived trilobite lineages.

ordo-046.title: The Ural Ocean forms
ordo-046.text: Large islands from Siberia collided with Baltica in the Late Ordovician, and the Ural Ocean formed between them. It was one more new basin in a world of shifting plates, where terranes were splitting from Gondwana and older oceans were closing. This ocean was only beginning its life.

ordo-047.title: Lockne and Målingen: twin craters in Sweden
ordo-047.text: An asteroid about 600 m across blasted the 7.5 km Lockne crater in what is now northern Sweden. Just 16 km away lies the smaller Målingen crater, which may be its twin, made by a body about 250 m across. Chitinozoan microfossils date the impact to about 458 million years ago.

ordo-048.title: The Kärdla crater, Estonia
ordo-048.text: About 455 million years ago, a meteorite struck what is now Estonia and left the 4 km Kärdla crater. It came during a time of frequent impacts in the Ordovician. Estonia, Sweden and North America all hold craters from this stretch of the period.

ordo-049.title: Deicke and Millbrig: ash falls bigger than Toba
ordo-049.text: The largest ash fall of the last 590 million years came down about 454 Ma. Huge eruptions during the Taconic orogeny, probably from a volcanic arc, buried Laurentia in ash. Today it survives as the Deicke and Millbrig bentonites, clays formed from altered volcanic ash. Millbrig was the larger. Each eruption's ash layer was larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.

ordo-052.title: The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion
ordo-052.text: The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion began just above the base of the Katian Stage, dated to 452.8 million years ago. Its base helps fix that boundary at Black Knob Ridge, Oklahoma. It works together with the first appearance of the graptolite Diplacanthograptus caudatus, giving geologists two markers to find the same moment.

ordo-050.title: The Boda warming event
ordo-050.text: In the early Katian, global temperatures rose briefly in what is called the Boda Event. The warmth built reef mounds and spread animals across Europe. It was a short warm spell in a cooling world, and it came before the great Hirnantian ice that ended the period.

ordo-051.title: Extinction rates rise in the Katian
ordo-051.text: The Late Ordovician extinction did not come out of nowhere. Extinction rates rose significantly in the early or middle Katian, several million years before the Hirnantian glaciation. This early phase is linked to large igneous province activity, possibly the Alborz province of northern Iran, and to the Boda event. Bryozoan losses were drawn out: extinction rates were higher in the early and late Katian, and new species appeared far less often late in the stage.

ordo-054.title: Arthropods walk onto land
ordo-054.text: The oldest clear evidence of animals on land belongs to arthropods, around 450 Ma. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods began colonizing land at least from the Ordovician. They may have thrived on food provided by early land plants. Late Ordovician trace fossils, a little over 445 Ma, probably record invertebrates living on land.

ordo-055.title: Avalonia collides with Baltica
ordo-055.text:
At about 30°S, eastern Avalonia rammed into Baltica and closed the Tornquist Sea between them. The collision formed the northwestern part of the Trans-European Suture Zone and coincided with the Shelveian orogeny of western England and Wales.

It also ended the Rheic Ocean's widening south of Avalonia. Huge magmatism followed in Avalonia, and a gigantic ash fall in Baltica. Avalonian magmatism peaked between 457 and 449 Ma.

ordo-056.title: The Charlevoix impact, Quebec
ordo-056.text: A stony meteorite struck what is now Charlevoix, Quebec, leaving a structure about 54 km across. Its age, 450 ± 20 million years, spans the Ordovician to the Silurian. The margin of error is wide enough that the impact cannot yet be placed in one period or the other.

ordo-053.title: The Alice Springs Orogeny tilts Uluru
ordo-053.text: Mountain building in central Australia lasted from about 450 Ma to about 300 Ma, far from any plate edge. The Alice Springs Orogeny shortened the crust north to south by under 100 km. Beginning in the Late Ordovician, it folded central Australian basins and had raised the MacDonnell Ranges by the Carboniferous. It may also have tilted the sandstone layers of Uluru to near vertical.

ordo-061.title: Deniliquin: an impact that might have triggered the ice
ordo-061.text: Deep under south-east Australia lies a buried structure of multiple rings at Deniliquin. It has been dated to around the start of the first extinction pulse. A 2023 paper proposed that an impact there caused an impact winter that triggered the Hirnantian glaciation and extinction. The idea remains untested, and the structure is not listed as a confirmed impact crater.

ordo-058.title: HICE: a carbon marker for the Hirnantian
ordo-058.text: Through the Hirnantian, a positive carbon isotope excursion, the HICE, ran alongside a short but large glaciation. Its cause is still debated. Its value is practical: it is a key marker for defining the Ordovician–Silurian boundary worldwide. Its exact age is uncertain, because the Hirnantian is short and dating errors are comparatively large.

ordo-059.title: The Hirnantian glaciation at its peak
ordo-059.text:
Sea level fell from about 220 m above today's to about 141 m. A sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary rapidly expanded glaciers in one of the most severe glaciations of the Phanerozoic. Ice caps covered Gondwana over the South Pole, in what is now Africa and South America. The cold was probably harsher than the Last Glacial Maximum.

The chemistry of the sea records the shock. Oxygen isotope ratios jumped by an extraordinary 2–4‰ at the start of the Hirnantian, and CO2 dropped sharply.

Then it ended as abruptly as it began. The ice retreated at the end of the Hirnantian, and Earth returned to a much warmer climate in the Rhuddanian. The cold and the thaw each brought their own wave of death, in {{ref:ordo-064}}.

ordo-060.title: The Hirnantian ocean loses its oxygen
ordo-060.text: As the glaciers retreated, black shales spread from isolated basins to all latitudes and depths, the mark of a global anoxic event. Repeated spells of anoxia mark the Ordovician–Silurian boundary. Anoxia is the most common suspect for the extinction's second pulse. Sudden volcanism may have supplied sulphur dioxide that favored euxinia, water both oxygen-free and rich in hydrogen sulfide. The Hirnantian–Rhuddanian anoxia may be one of the longest-lasting anoxic events in geologic time, and its cause is uncertain.

ordo-062.title: Beecher's Trilobite Bed: soft parts in gold
ordo-062.text: The soft parts of trilobites rarely survive, but in a thin shale bed in Oneida County, New York, they do. Trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni have their soft tissues replaced by pyrite, fool's gold. The bed ranks among the world's best examples of near-perfect fossil preservation.

ordo-063.title: The first jawed fish
ordo-063.text: The jaw may have appeared in the Late Ordovician, about 445 Ma. The first jawed vertebrates, or gnathostomes, arose from among the armored jawless ostracoderms. The earliest evidence is microscopic. Late Ordovician scale microfossils, possibly from acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', are the oldest signs of jawed fish. They took time to flourish. Jawed fish became common only in the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes'.

ordo-064.title: The Late Ordovician mass extinction
ordo-064.text:
Only one extinction in Earth's history was larger. The Late Ordovician mass extinction, the first of the 'Big Five', removed by various estimates from about 60% of marine genera to 85% of marine species. Only the end-Permian extinction surpassed it.

It came in two pulses. The first, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary, is tied to the sudden Hirnantian glaciation. The second, later in the Hirnantian, came with warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated.

Trilobites lost about 70% of their genera and 50% of their families. Many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished. Yet for all its severity, it changed the structure of ecosystems little, and diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.

silu-001.title: Armorica drifts away from Gondwana
silu-001.text: The Armorican Terrane Assemblage, a set of crustal blocks that now lie in western Europe, split away from Gondwana in the Silurian. Its complete separation, across the young Paleo-Tethys, is thought to have come toward the end of the period. Through the Devonian it drifted toward Laurussia. Late in the Carboniferous it collided with Laurussia in the Variscan orogeny.

silu-002.title: Armored jawless fish reach their peak
silu-002.text:
By the Late Silurian, armored jawless fish, the ostracoderms, had reached the high point of their evolution. Anaspids appear in the early Silurian. Osteostracans, probably arising in Euramerica, appear in the Llandovery or Wenlock. Thelodont scales turn up worldwide, and the tadpole-like archipelepidiforms lived from the late Telychian to the Sheinwoodian. Heterostracans of the order Traquairaspidiformes appear in the Late Silurian.

Their success was short. The Silurian rise of jawed fish coincided with a sharp decline of jawless forms such as conodonts and ostracoderms.

silu-003.title: The asaphid trilobites die out
silu-003.text: Asaphida, a large and varied trilobite order known since the Middle Cambrian, died out during the Silurian. Its last members, the Trinucleioidea, disappeared before the end of the period. Their loss closed a lineage that had lasted through the whole of the Ordovician and its great extinction.

silu-004.title: The Clinton ironstones of the Appalachians
silu-004.text: From New York to Alabama, layers of shale, mudstone, sandstone and iron-rich rock built up in the Appalachian Foreland Basin in the early Silurian. These are the Clinton Group and its 'Clinton Ironstones'. They are richly fossiliferous, an important record of early Silurian marine life. They are best known, though, as a significant source of iron ore.

silu-009.title: Jawed fish diversify
silu-009.text:
The fish families of today's oceans began in the Silurian. A major milestone of the period was the diversification of jawed fish: placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish. Cartilaginous and bony fish, the jawed groups still alive, appeared by the late Silurian.

The branching was fast. By about 419 Ma, jawed fish had split into placoderms, bony fish, and a group joining the spiny sharks with the cartilaginous fish. The placoderm Entelognathus already had a bony jaw skeleton. Lobe-finned fish, or Sarcopterygii, emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian, all still living in water.

Fish diversified greatly through the Silurian and Devonian. Even so, they produced fewer new body plans than animals did in the Cambrian explosion.

silu-011.title: The last dissidocerid cephalopods
silu-011.text: Dissidocerida, an order of cephalopods with straight shells, had lived since the Early Ordovician. Its last appearance is in the Early Silurian. The order was one of several that arose in the Ordovician heyday of the nautiloids and faded after the period's great extinction.

silu-012.title: The last eocrinoids
silu-012.text: Eocrinoids, the early stalked echinoderms, had been around since Cambrian Stage 3. They make their last appearance in the Silurian. Once the most common echinoderms of the Cambrian, they outlasted the end-Ordovician extinction before finally disappearing.

silu-013.title: The last nektaspid arthropods
silu-013.text: Nektaspida, trilobite-like arthropods without mineral shells, had lived since the early Cambrian. They last appear in the upper Silurian. Because their bodies were not mineralized, they are known only from sites of exceptional preservation, which makes their long survival easy to overlook.

silu-014.title: The last paracrinoids
silu-014.text: Paracrinoids, echinoderms of shallow seas, lived from the Early Ordovician to the Early Silurian. They were among the new classes of the Ordovician echinoderm radiation, and among the first of those classes to vanish. Their span covers barely more than one period.

silu-016.title: Stromatoporoid sponges branch out
silu-016.text: Most stromatoporoid sponge orders, including Amphiporida and Stromatoporida, originated in the Silurian. Clathrodictyids and actinostromatids diversified strongly while the older labechiids declined. Amphiporida is first recorded in the Ludlow. These sponges helped build the expanding reefs of the period.

silu-017.title: Nematophytes tower over early plants
silu-017.text: The tallest things on Silurian land were not true plants. Nematophytes, a loose group of land organisms including some plants and algae, towered over even the largest land plants. They formed networks of large, mycorrhizal forms, living in partnership with fungi. Nematothallus is first recorded in the Ludfordian, alongside Cooksonia in Ludlow rocks. They lasted into the Early Devonian, and truly larger plants came only in the Early Carboniferous.

silu-019.title: The Rheic Ocean at its widest
silu-019.text: As Avalonia and Carolina drifted north from Gondwana, the ocean behind them kept widening. In the Silurian, the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width, about 4,000 km. It separated Laurussia to the north from Gondwana to the south. From then on it could only narrow.

silu-020.title: Dob's Linn: where the Silurian begins
silu-020.text: In a small valley in southern Scotland, Dob's Linn, lies the reference section for the Ordovician–Silurian boundary and the base of the Llandovery. The boundary is set where two graptolites, Parakidograptus acuminatus and Akidograptus ascensus, first appear in the Birkhill Shale. It follows the end-Ordovician extinctions, which wiped out up to 60% of marine genera.

silu-015.title: Life rebounds after the end-Ordovician extinction
silu-015.text:
Animals that seemed extinct came back. Many 'Lazarus taxa' missing from the latest Ordovician reappeared in the Silurian, so small populations must have survived in refuges.

As melting ice raised sea level and re-flooded the continental shelves, biodiversity rebounded within the surviving orders. Early Silurian communities were simpler and broader in their habits, but faunas became among the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic. Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors in the earliest Rhuddanian. Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian, while pentamerid brachiopods waited until the Aeronian. Bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

silu-006.title: The first placoderms, armored jawed fish
silu-006.text: The vertebrate jaw probably evolved in the Silurian, and it appeared in placoderms, armored jawed fish. The first identifiable placoderms appear in the late Llandovery. Their Silurian record is fragmentary, probably because they lived where fossils rarely formed. A rare near-complete find is the antiarch Silurolepis, from Ludlow rocks of Yunnan. Placoderms diversified further in the Devonian.

silu-010.title: Land plants spread across the continents
silu-010.text: Mercury isotopes in the rocks show that by the Early Silurian, land plants had spread across much of Earth's land surface. Plants were already moving onto land in the Llandovery. Eohostimella, probably a land plant, is known from rocks about 440–430 Ma, and spores and plant microfossils of this age come from China and Pennsylvania. Silurian floras were broadly similar across the globe, with little regional difference.

silu-018.title: Silurian reefs spread to high latitudes
silu-018.text: Silurian barrier reefs covered much more seafloor than reefs do today, and they grew even at high latitudes. Widespread reef building began in the Llandovery and continued into the Devonian. Tabulate corals formed prominent mounds. Coral photosymbiosis, a partnership with light-using algae, may have begun in the Llandovery, and corals with it appear by the Middle Silurian. Hederelloids flourished, some living in symbiosis with the rugose coral Entelophyllum.

silu-024.title: The Taconic orogeny comes to an end
silu-024.text: The Taconic orogeny, which built mountains across New England, ended about 440 Ma. Subduction stopped, and the Iapetus Terrane was welded onto eastern North America. Then erosion took over. Through the Silurian and Devonian, sediment from the wearing mountains spread over the Appalachians and the North American midcontinent.

silu-023.title: Silurian glaciers shift to South America
silu-023.text: After the Hirnantian ice age, milder glaciations continued through the Silurian, the last in the Late Silurian. The center of glaciation moved from the Sahara to South America, with ice recorded in Arabia, West Africa, the Amazon and the Andes. Glacial phases struck in the early and latest Aeronian, the late Telychian to mid-Sheinwoodian, the Homerian and the Ludfordian. The ice caps were smaller than the Late Ordovician ones, and glaciers almost vanished by mid-Silurian. A lack of tillites, glacial deposits turned to rock, in the middle to late Silurian makes ice a problematic explanation for its climate swings.

silu-025.title: The oldest unambiguous jawed fish
silu-025.text: Teeth and scales from Guizhou, China, about 439 Ma, are the oldest unambiguous remains of jawed vertebrates. They belong to Qianodus and Fanjingshania, from Aeronian rocks. Both are acanthodian-grade stem chondrichthyans, early relatives of the cartilaginous fish; possibly older Ordovician records exist. Acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', arose about 50 million years before the first true sharks. By the early Silurian, jawed-vertebrate fossils, mostly primitive acanthodians, are unmistakable, and by the Devonian they are abundant.

silu-026.title: Chongqing: complete early jawed fish
silu-026.text: Near Chongqing, China, the Huixingshao Formation, about 436 Ma, preserves complete fossils of the earliest jawed vertebrates. It also holds galeaspids, a group of jawless fish, and eurypterids. One fish of this age, Shenacanthus, had armor plates on its chest like those of placoderms, a hint of how early jawed fish mixed features.

silu-027.title: The first bony fish
silu-027.text:
Every land vertebrate descends from a fish with bones. The oldest known bony-fish fossils, about 436 million years old, have teeth arranged midway between those of sharks and those of true bony fish. Their skeletons were still mostly cartilage. Their novelty was foregut pouches that later became swim bladders and lungs.

Bony fish appeared in the Silurian and became common and diverse in the Devonian. One branch, the lobe-finned fish, later gave rise to all land vertebrates. Guiyu oneiros, about 425 Ma from Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest articulated bony fish. It mixes placoderm-like traits with those of ray- and lobe-finned fish.

silu-029.title: The Scandian collision of Baltica and Laurentia
silu-029.text:
The edge of Baltica was dragged about 120 km down into the Earth around 429 Ma, deep enough to form micro-diamonds. This was the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny, when Baltica and Laurentia collided from about 435 to 410 Ma.

Avalonia, Baltica and Laurentia drifted together near the equator and began to form Euramerica. The collision folded coastal sediments that had built up for ages, raising mountains from New York State through Greenland and Britain to Norway. Thrusting built Scotland's Moine Thrust Belt, 435–420 Ma, and in Scandinavia great sheets of rock called nappes stacked on top of one another.

Life noticed the closing ocean. Trilobite faunas from both sides mixed as the water between them narrowed.

silu-031.title: Cooksonia, the first vascular plant
silu-031.text:
A small Silurian plant carries one of evolution's great inventions. Cooksonia, the oldest known vascular plant, appears in the Wenlock, in the middle of the Silurian. Vascular plants, or tracheophytes, have internal tubes that carry water through their bodies.

Cooksonia lasted. It remained an important part of the flora until the end of the Early Devonian, spanning 433 to 393 Ma. One species from about 432 Ma, C. barrandei, is known from its spore-bearing stage, the sporophyte. Most rocks that hold it are marine, so the plants probably grew along rivers and streams.

They may not have been the first. Slightly later, more complex plants from Gondwana such as Baragwanathia suggest vascular plants have a longer history, perhaps reaching into the early Silurian.

silu-032.title: The Ireviken extinction event
silu-032.text:
In about 200,000 years, 80% of conodont species vanished worldwide. The Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, struck at the Llandovery–Wenlock boundary. At Ireviken on Gotland, over half the trilobite species died out.

It began in the deep ocean and spread to the shelf seas. Graptolites, conodonts and trilobites suffered most, while shallow reefs were barely touched. It is linked to global cooling, and {{ref:silu-035}} followed. Its eight extinction steps appear to track Milankovitch cycles, regular wobbles in Earth's orbit. Its sediments show enrichment in metals.

silu-033.title: The last bisonocerid nautiloids
silu-033.text: Bisonocerida, a nautiloid order dating from the Tremadocian, last appears in the Wenlock. It had arisen in the Early Ordovician, when nautiloids were at their height, and lasted through the end-Ordovician extinction before disappearing. Its end is one more sign of the slow fading of the old Ordovician nautiloid groups.

silu-035.title: Carbon spikes after the Ireviken event
silu-035.text: After the first Ireviken extinctions, the carbon isotope value δ13C rose from +1.4‰ to +4.5‰. Oxygen isotopes rose too, from −5.6‰ to −5.0‰. This early Silurian excursion, about 431 Ma, resembles the Cambrian SPICE event, peaking near +4.5‰. The Silurian had more such isotope excursions, a sign of climate swings, than any other period.

silu-036.title: The Lundgreni event
silu-036.text: Graptolite diversity hit a global low in the middle Homerian, and the cyrtograptids died out. This was the Lundgreni event, or Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis, recorded in Iberia, Bohemia and Poland. It hit graptolites, seafloor animals and microscopic plankton hardest. Eutrophication, an overload of nutrients, and anoxia are blamed. A double-peaked positive carbon isotope excursion began with it.

silu-038.title: The first scorpions
silu-038.text: Scorpions date back to the Silurian, about 430 Ma. The oldest known, Dolichophonus loudonensis, lived in what is now Scotland. Whether early scorpions lived in water or on land is debated, though early forms like Eramoscorpius had book lungs, stacked plates for breathing air. Land scorpions appear in timelines at about 420 Ma.

silu-039.title: The Great Glen Fault cuts across Scotland
silu-039.text: The Scottish Highlands take their shape from a fault. The Great Glen Fault formed late in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia and Baltica collided, probably between 430 and 390 Ma. It is a product of the same collision that raised mountains from Norway to New York.

silu-041.title: Oxygen climbs to modern levels
silu-041.text:
In the early Silurian, oxygen stood near 13% of today's level; by the Devonian it approached modern levels. This stepwise rise to and above modern levels, the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event, ran from about 428 to 359 Ma, alongside the spread of vascular plants.

Plants likely drove it. Their higher photosynthetic yield released more oxygen, and burying organic carbon in rocks cut the oxygen sink. Carbon trapped in rock also meant less CO2 in the air, and the climate cooled.

silu-042.title: The Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution
silu-042.text:
The continents turned green. From 428 to 359 Ma, land plants, especially vascular plants, and fungi rapidly colonized and diversified on dry land. The critical phase came in the Late Silurian and Early Devonian.

Vascular plants arose from simpler land plants. Fungi spread, and myriapods, arachnids and hexapods became fully terrestrial. Plant diversity rose on a scale compared with the Cambrian explosion of animals, notably in tall, woody vascular plants that later formed canopies. Volcanic islands of the Rheic Ocean were hotspots of plant evolution.

The new vegetation reshaped the water cycle and the global climate. It changed ocean nutrients and sediment cycling worldwide, likely feeding plankton blooms tied to the Late Devonian extinction.

silu-043.title: The Mulde extinction event
silu-043.text: The Mulde event, an anoxic event, was the second of three relatively minor Silurian mass extinctions. It coincided with a global drop in sea level and was closely followed by an isotope excursion. Carbon isotopes suggest a sustained drop in CO2 at the time. Its onset matches the Fröjel Formation of Gotland. Some apparent conodont losses may reflect changed sediments rather than real extinction.

prot-119.text: A rock of jumbled glacial rubble, unsorted grains and stones of all sizes.

camb-080.text: A tube running through the chambers of a cephalopod shell.

camb-073.text: Tiny animals that live among the grains of the seafloor.

ordo-060.text: Water that is both free of oxygen and rich in hydrogen sulfide.

ordo-049.text: A clay formed from altered volcanic ash.
